[Field Guide]{.type-badge}

In the autumn of 2025, two companies most people had never heard of taught the market a
lesson about what it didn't know. **Tricolor Holdings**, a Dallas subprime auto lender,
collapsed into Chapter 7 amid allegations its executives had pledged the same auto-loan
collateral to several banks at once; JPMorgan and Fifth Third took writedowns, and Jamie
Dimon offered the season's motif — when you see one cockroach, there are usually more. Weeks
later **First Brands**, an auto-parts maker, filed with more than $10 billion in liabilities
after a tangle of off-balance-sheet financing turned out to rest on inflated invoices and
near-empty special-purpose vehicles.

Neither was, on its face, systemic. But both pointed a spotlight at the same question:
**how exposed is any given bank to private credit — and can an outsider actually measure it
before the headlines?**

The answer is yes, more than you'd expect — with two limits we'll come to. The raw material
sits in free public filings. This guide walks the two levels at which you read them: the
**market in aggregate**, then a **single bank** — using two deliberately different banks to
show that the technique changes with how much a bank chooses to tell you. Every number below
is computed live from the FDIC's public API; the code is in the margins.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

_panel = pd.read_parquet(Path("../../analysis/outputs/call_report_ndfi_panel.parquet"))
_agg = pd.read_parquet(Path("../../analysis/outputs/ndfi_aggregate_series.parquet"))

_latest = _panel["quarter"].max()
_cur = _panel[_panel["quarter"] == _latest].copy()

# Roll subsidiary banks up to the top-tier holding company. Many companies file
# through several bank subs (Wells Fargo 5, Morgan Stanley 2, BNY 4), which would
# otherwise show up as duplicate points and double-labelled banks.
_cur["entity"] = _cur["NAMEHCR"].str.strip()
_cur.loc[_cur["entity"] == "", "entity"] = _cur["NAME"]
_g = _cur.groupby("entity").agg(
    ndfi=("LNNDEPC", "sum"), tier1=("RBCT1J", "sum"),
    assets=("ASSET", "sum"), loans=("LNLSNET", "sum"),
    certs=("CERT", lambda s: set(s)),
).reset_index()
_g["ndfi_to_tier1"] = _g["ndfi"] / _g["tier1"]
_g["ndfi_to_loans"] = _g["ndfi"] / _g["loans"]
_g["ndfi_bn"] = _g["ndfi"] / 1e6
_g["asset_bn"] = _g["assets"] / 1e6
_g["example"] = _g["certs"].apply(lambda s: bool({11063, 9846} & s))

_fix = {
    "Jpmorgan Chase&Co": "JPMorgan Chase", "Bank Of America Corp": "Bank of America",
    "Wells Fargo&Company": "Wells Fargo", "Goldman Sachs Group Inc The": "Goldman Sachs",
    "Citigroup Inc": "Citigroup", "Pnc Finl Services Group Inc": "PNC",
    "U S Bcorp": "U.S. Bancorp", "Truist Financial Corp": "Truist",
    "First Citizens Bancshares Inc": "First Citizens", "Capital One Financial Corp": "Capital One",
    "State Street Corp": "State Street", "Keycorp": "KeyCorp",
    "Bank Of Ny Mellon Corp The": "BNY Mellon", "Charles Schwab Corp The": "Charles Schwab",
    "Fifth Third Bancorp": "Fifth Third", "Citizens Financial Group Inc": "Citizens",
    "Regions Financial Corp": "Regions", "American Express Co": "American Express",
    "Northern Trust Corp": "Northern Trust", "Morgan Stanley": "Morgan Stanley",
    "Huntington Bancshares Inc": "Huntington", "Bank Of Montreal": "BMO",
    "M&T Bank Corp": "M&T Bank",
}
_g["label"] = _g["entity"].str.title().replace(_fix)

_rank_df = _g[_g["ndfi_bn"] >= 10].sort_values("ndfi_to_tier1", ascending=False).head(18)
ranking = [{"bank": r.label, "ratio": float(r.ndfi_to_tier1), "ndfi": float(r.ndfi_bn),
            "example": bool(r.example)} for r in _rank_df.itertuples()]
scatter = [{"bank": r.label, "ndfi": float(r.ndfi_bn), "ratio": float(r.ndfi_to_tier1),
            "assets": float(r.asset_bn), "example": bool(r.example)}
           for r in _g.itertuples() if pd.notna(r.ndfi_to_tier1)]
market = [{"quarter": str(pd.Timestamp(r.quarter).date()), "total": float(r.ndfi_total_bn),
           "top10": float(r.top10_share)} for r in _agg.itertuples()]
composition = [{"slice": "Capital-call lines", "pct": 0.85, "alll": 0.09},
               {"slice": "Other NDFI / private credit", "pct": 0.15, "alll": 1.06}]

# a few figures for the prose
_last = _agg.iloc[-1]
mkt_total = f"${_last.ndfi_total_bn/1000:.1f} trillion"
mkt_top10 = f"{_last.top10_share:.0%}"
mkt_big = f"{_last.big_bank_share:.0%}"
mkt_n = int(_last.n_reporters)
_tfc = _g[_g["certs"].apply(lambda s: 9846 in s)].iloc[0]
_fcnca = _g[_g["certs"].apply(lambda s: 11063 in s)].iloc[0]

ojs_define(ranking=ranking, scatter=scatter, market=market, composition=composition)
```

---

## Part 1 — Reading the market in aggregate

Before judging any one bank, get a feel for the whole system: its size, its growth, its
concentration, its stress level. The workhorse is a single free line item.

Bank exposure to private credit lives mostly under one Call Report category: **loans to
non-depository financial institutions (NDFIs)** — funds, BDCs, private-credit vehicles,
insurers, broker-dealers. Since 2024-Q4, every bank over $10 billion in assets reports it
directly, and the FDIC serves it through a public API. Summing that one field across every
bank gives you the market:

```python
# every bank's NDFI balance for one quarter, from the free FDIC API
import urllib.request, json
url = ("https://api.fdic.gov/banks/financials?filters=REPDTE:20260331"
       "&fields=CERT,NAMEHCR,ASSET,LNLSNET,LNNDEPC,RBCT1J&limit=10000&format=json")
recs = [d["data"] for d in json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(url))["data"]]
ndfi = [r for r in recs if r.get("LNNDEPC")]          # ~80 banks report it
total = sum(r["LNNDEPC"] for r in ndfi) / 1e6         # -> $1,484 billion
```

That sum is the headline scoreboard. As of Q1 2026, drawn bank exposure to NDFIs was roughly
**`{python} mkt_total`** across **`{python} mkt_n` reporting banks** — computed above, and it
matches the FDIC's own Quarterly Banking Profile aggregate. On top of the *drawn* balance
sits undrawn firepower: counting unused commitments, independent estimates
([Whalen's *Institutional Risk Analyst*](https://www.theinstitutionalriskanalyst.com/)) put
*potential* exposure-at-default near **$3 trillion**. That gap is the most under-appreciated
fact in the subject — most NDFI lending revolves, so the on-balance-sheet number understates
true exposure, and stress is exactly when borrowers draw the rest.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<figure class="jc-fig">${chartMarket}<figcaption>Drawn bank loans to non-depository financial institutions, summed across all reporting banks. <span class="ill">Real data — FDIC BankFind financials API, bank-level Call Report, Q4 2024–Q1 2026.</span></figcaption></figure>`
```

Two structural facts fall straight out of the same pull:

- **Concentration.** Banks over $100 billion in assets hold **`{python} mkt_big`** of all
  reported NDFI loans; the top ten alone hold **`{python} mkt_top10`**. This is a big-bank
  story first.
- **The deceptively calm quality metric.** The aggregate NDFI delinquency/loss rate is
  extraordinarily low — around 0.14%, the cleanest of any major loan category. That is the
  central tension: the fastest-growing lending is also, on paper, the best-performing. An
  optimist reads that as genuine safety; a skeptic reads it as reported quality lagging a
  book that hasn't been tested through a downturn. Both live in the same number.

One quirk to know before going bank-by-bank: the NDFI series only *begins* in Q4 2024, and
the earliest quarters are muddied by reclassification — loans were moved *into* the NDFI
buckets from other categories, so early "growth" is partly an accounting artifact. Prefer
the later quarters for genuine reads.

---

## The bridge — scale is not concentration

Here is where an outsider gets an edge. Plot every reporting bank by **how many NDFI dollars
it lends** (across) against **how large that book is relative to its Tier 1 capital** (up) —
the metric that actually matters for solvency. The two are *not* the same axis, and the
picture is not what the headlines suggest.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<figure class="jc-fig jc-wide">${chartScatter}<div class="jc-legend-r"><span class="jc-legend-lbl">Bubble = total assets</span>${sizeLegend}</div><figcaption>Every holding company reporting NDFI loans, Q1 2026. Horizontal = size of the book (log); vertical = book ÷ Tier 1 capital; bubble = total assets. <b>Hover any bubble for the bank.</b> Subsidiary banks rolled up to the holding company. <span class="ill">Real data; First Citizens &amp; Truist in orange.</span></figcaption></figure>`
```

The megabanks (JPMorgan, Wells, Bank of America) sit far to the right — they lend the most
*dollars* — but mostly below the 100%-of-capital line. The genuinely *concentrated* lenders
are elsewhere: the investment and custody banks (Goldman, Morgan Stanley, State Street) and
one deceptively small commercial bank, **First Citizens**, floating near the top. Dollars
tell you who matters to the system; the ratio tells you who is standing closest to the mine.
That distinction is the whole game — and it sets up the two banks.

---

## Part 2 — The concentrated specialist: First Citizens

**Why this bank.** First Citizens absorbed Silicon Valley Bank's fund-banking business, and
it shows: NDFI lending runs about a third of its entire commercial book. When a bank is this
concentrated, the exposure *is* the story — and, crucially, it knows investors will ask, so
it discloses in detail. **The method here is the easy one: read the disclosure.**

The direct line confirms the scale: First Citizens reported NDFI loans of
**$`{python} f"{_fcnca.ndfi_bn:.1f}"` billion** — about
**`{python} f"{_fcnca.ndfi_to_loans:.0%}"`** of its total loans, and, against a comparatively
small capital base, **`{python} f"{_fcnca.ndfi_to_tier1:.0%}"` of Tier 1 capital.** That is
the highest concentration of any large commercial bank in the country. But the *composition*
is what turns a scary headline into a defensible book, and the bank breaks it out:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<figure class="jc-fig comp">
  <div class="comp-bar">
    <div class="comp-seg" style="width:85%;background:${INK}">85%</div>
    <div class="comp-seg" style="width:15%;background:${HI}">15%</div>
  </div>
  <div class="comp-cards">
    <div class="comp-card">
      <div class="comp-share" style="color:${INK}">85%</div>
      <div class="comp-name">Capital-call lines</div>
      <div class="comp-desc">Secured by the contractual capital commitments of a fund's limited partners — pensions, endowments, sovereign wealth — <em>not</em> by the fund's investments. Structurally the safest slice.</div>
      <div class="comp-alll">Allowance for losses<b style="color:${INK}">0.09%</b></div>
    </div>
    <div class="comp-card comp-card--risk">
      <div class="comp-share" style="color:${HI}">15%</div>
      <div class="comp-name">Other NDFI / private credit</div>
      <div class="comp-desc">Traditional private-credit and NAV-based lending, where any real valuation risk in the book actually lives.</div>
      <div class="comp-alll">Allowance for losses<b style="color:${HI}">1.06%</b></div>
    </div>
  </div>
  <figcaption>First Citizens' NDFI book by type, per its FY2025 10-K. The <b>12× allowance gap</b> between the two slices is the evidence behind its "big but safe" framing. <span class="ill">Disclosed figures; holding-company basis.</span></figcaption>
</figure>`
```

- **Capital-call lines — ~85% of the book (~$31.8B).** Secured against the contractual
  capital commitments of a fund's limited partners (pensions, endowments, sovereign wealth),
  *not* against the performance of the fund's investments — structurally the safest slice.
- **Other NDFI / traditional private credit — the remaining ~15% (~$5.8B),** where any real
  valuation risk lives.

And the bank hands you a **loss-rate contrast that substantiates its own safety claim:** the
allowance was just **0.09% on capital-call lines versus 1.06% on total loans**. That gap is
the evidence behind management's "this looks big but it's safe" framing. The outsider's job
is to check whether the provisioning matches the story — here it does, so far. What to watch
is the *trend, not the level*: First Citizens' nonaccrual ratio ticked up to ~96 bps in
Q1 2026, which management called isolated — exactly the claim you verify over the next two or
three quarters rather than accept or dismiss at once.

---

## Part 3 — The diversified bank: Truist, and the proxy that overstated

**Why this bank.** Truist is large and diversified, and NDFI is *not* a headline for it.
Historically you couldn't read it off the filing at all — you had to **infer** it. The
classic technique, popularized by Whalen's *Institutional Risk Analyst*, used the Call
Report's broad **"Other Loans & Leases" (OLL)** line as a proxy and measured it against Tier
1 capital. On that proxy, Truist's book came out near **130% of Tier 1** — an alarming
number.

Now there's a direct line, and it tells a different story. Computing the real NDFI figure
the same way we did the aggregate — just one bank, one division:

```python
truist = next(r for r in ndfi if r["CERT"] == 9846)
concentration = truist["LNNDEPC"] / truist["RBCT1J"]   # NDFI ÷ Tier 1  ->  0.77
```

Truist's **direct** NDFI exposure is **$`{python} f"{_tfc.ndfi_bn:.1f}"` billion** —
**`{python} f"{_tfc.ndfi_to_loans:.0%}"`** of loans and just
**`{python} f"{_tfc.ndfi_to_tier1:.0%}"` of Tier 1 capital.** That is the finding: the OLL
proxy said 130%; the direct line says `{python} f"{_tfc.ndfi_to_tier1:.0%}"`. OLL is a
*broader* bucket — NDFI is only about 60% of it system-wide — so the old proxy
systematically **overstated** true private-credit concentration. It was the right tool when
it was the only tool; it is not the right tool anymore. When you can read the direct line,
read it.

That is the deeper lesson of the two banks, made literal in one ranking. Sort every large
NDFI lender by concentration-to-capital, and the two case studies land exactly where the
method predicts — First Citizens near the top, Truist comfortably in the pack:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<figure class="jc-fig">${chartRank}<figcaption>NDFI loans as a share of Tier 1 capital, Q1 2026, banks with over $10B in NDFI. The dashed line is 100% — a book equal to the bank's entire tier 1 capital. <span class="ill">Real data; case-study banks in orange.</span></figcaption></figure>`
```

The surprise is at the top: it is the **investment and custody banks** — Goldman, Morgan
Stanley, State Street — not the big commercial lenders, that run the most concentrated NDFI
books relative to capital. That is not a headline anyone is writing, and it took nothing but
a free API and one division to see it.

---

## What the two examples teach

The contrast is the lesson. **First Citizens** is the *rich-disclosure* path: a concentrated
specialist that must explain itself, where the 10-K hands you the capital-call split and a
loss-rate contrast you can check. **Truist** is the *inference-being-retired* path: a
diversified bank you used to reconstruct from a proxy, now readable directly — and the proxy,
it turns out, was running hot. Most banks fall between these two, and the same three-number
recipe places any of them: **NDFI ÷ Tier 1** for concentration, the **capital-call vs.
everything-else** split for composition, and the **loss-rate contrast** for whether the
provisioning matches the story.

Two honest limits belong at the end. First, the per-bank series only begins with the Q4 2024
Call Report, and the early quarters are muddied by reclassification — apparent "growth" in
that window is partly an accounting artifact, not new lending. Second, and more fundamental:
public data measures *reported* condition. The failures that defined 2025 — double-pledged
collateral at Tricolor, fabricated invoices at First Brands — were deliberate misreporting.
No delinquency field would have caught them, because until the day of collapse the loans
looked current. Public data can't tell you whether these cases are idiosyncratic or the
canary in the coal mine. What it *can* do — market-wide, and bank by bank — is tell you who
is standing closest to the mine. For an outsider, that is a great deal more than nothing.

::: {.ill-note}
**Data & method.** All figures computed from the **FDIC BankFind financials API** (free, no
key) at the **bank level** — NDFI = Call Report field `LNNDEPC`, Tier 1 capital = `RBCT1J`,
Q1 2026. Case-study composition and loss-rate figures are from First Citizens' FY2025 10-K
and are **holding-company** basis; the two levels are labeled and never divided by each
other. Pull and aggregation scripts: `analysis/pull_call_reports.py`,
`analysis/aggregate_ndfi.py`. The ~130% OLL proxy for Truist is Whalen's *Institutional Risk
Analyst*, cited; reproducing it independently needs the FFIEC Call Report "Other Loans &
Leases" line — a follow-up.
:::
